passage: Dada was on the verandah again, tapping his stick. "Always carry a cloth for the sun, Sudha. And never trust the second offer." Sudha had heard it forty times. She rolled her eyes and muttered, "Dada, that was your time, not now." His stick went quiet. The village lane was dusty and the buffalo bell clanked far away. Sudha felt a small pinch in her chest. That evening she sat next to him and said, "I am sorry, Dada. I will take the cloth. Tell me about the second offer." His eyes crinkled. She still planned to choose her own school bag, but she listened.

qa.q: What did Dada tell Sudha to always carry?
qa.a: He told her to always carry a cloth for the sun.

qa.q: What made Sudha feel a small pinch in her chest?
qa.a: She had rolled her eyes and spoken rudely, and when the stick went quiet she realised she had hurt her grandfather.

qa.q: What could Sudha do the next time the advice feels old-fashioned?
qa.a: She can listen patiently, thank him and still make her own choices, without rolling her eyes or answering rudely.

qa.q: How might Dada have felt when Sudha said, "that was your time, not now"?
qa.a: Dada probably felt dismissed and a little hurt, which is why his tapping stopped.

grounding: A child irritated by her grandfather's repeated advice answers rudely, feels the cost, and listens patiently while keeping her own choices.

passage: 'Zeenat, don't take the shortcut by the canal, the mud is slippery,' Dadajaan said from his charpai, for the third time that morning. Zeenat rolled her eyes so hard that Jahnavi, waiting at the gate, giggled. 'I know, Dadajaan! You say it every single day!' The words came out sharper than she meant. Dadajaan went quiet and looked down at his prayer beads. All the way to school, taking the long road round, Zeenat felt a pinch in her chest. The canal path was slippery, actually. And he said it because he had fallen there once, years ago. That afternoon she sat beside his charpai. 'Sorry for snapping. Tell me again about when you fell?' He smiled and told her, and she listened, even though she knew the story.

qa.q: Which shortcut did Dadajaan warn about?
What was Zeenat feeling on the long road to school?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy about snapping at Dadajaan, who had gone quiet.
She said sorry and asked to hear his story again, listening patiently even though she knew it.

qa.q: How might Dadajaan have felt when Zeenat snapped?
qa.a: Hurt and a little embarrassed; he went quiet and looked down at his prayer beads.

grounding: A village girl irritated by her grandfather's repeated advice snaps at him, then apologises and listens.

passage: Every morning in their Hanoi apartment, Ông said the same thing as Tuan tied his shoes: 'Wear the jacket. The wind gets into your chest.' Tuan was eleven and never felt cold. Today his friend Emil, visiting from Denmark, was waiting at the door, and Tuan felt his cheeks go warm. He almost said, 'Ông, you're so old-fashioned.' He could feel the words in his mouth. Instead he took a breath. 'Thank you, Ông. I'll keep it in my bag, and if I'm cold, I'll wear it.' Ông nodded, satisfied. On the stairs Emil said, 'My grandma tells me the same thing about hats.' Tuan laughed. At evening football, the wind picked up. He pulled on the jacket and said nothing, but he smiled.

qa.q: Where did Tuan say he'd keep the jacket?
What was Tuan feeling when Ông repeated the advice in front of Emil?
qa.a: Embarrassed and irritated, almost calling Ông old-fashioned.

qa.q: What did Tuan do instead of a rude reply?
qa.a: He thanked Ông and made his own choice: carry the jacket and wear it if he got cold.

qa.q: How did Ông feel about Tuan's answer?

grounding: A boy irritated by his grandfather's repeated advice listens politely and still makes his own choice.
